Hmm, the "adj" case: the two prefixes are 2001:db8::/48 and 2001:db9::/48. Are they adjacent? 2001:db8::/48 covers [20010db800000000, 20010db800010000) — that's only a /48 range (65536 keys), not up to 20010db900000000. So they're NOT adjacent. My bad. Let me construct truly adjacent ranges: 2001:db8::/47 covers [20010db800000000, 20010dba00000000); and 2001:dbA::/47 covers [20010dba00000000, 20010dbc00000000). Hmm, 2001:db8::/47 → the 47th bit... upper bits: 20010db8 = 0010 0000 0000 0001 0000 1101 1011 1000. /47 means the top 47 bits of the 64-bit prefix are fixed; the mask clears the low 17 bits of the upper-64. 20010db800000000 & ~((1<<17)-1) = 20010db800000000 ✓. Range = [20010db800000000, 20010db800000000 + 2^17) = [20010db800000000, 20010db800020000). The next adjacent range with the same length: 2001:db8:0:2::/47 → [20010db800020000, 20010db800040000).

So use "2001:db8::/47 5" and "2001:db8:0:2::/47 5" → adjacent, same pair (5,47) → the boundary at 20010db800020000 must be dropped.

Let me test that. Both the C++ and reference agree in the previous tests anyway, but let me explicitly confirm the redundant endpoint is dropped.

Everything else looks right. UBSan error suite passes (143).

Let me run that adjacency test.
